opus-5.5.text:
I think when the benchmark numbers start to converge, it actually tells you more about the benchmarks than about the models. Most evaluations measure whether a model can get a well-defined answer to a well-defined question. Once everyone has learned how to do that reasonably well, the scores saturate, and the real differences move somewhere the benchmarks don't look.

For me, the differences show up in a few places.

The first is long-horizon behavior. A model can be great at a single-turn math problem or a coding puzzle, but what happens when you give it a messy task that takes fifty steps, where it has to recover from its own mistakes, decide what to look up, and know when to stop? Two models with the same score on a static benchmark can behave completely differently there. One stays coherent, the other drifts.

The second is what I'd call taste, or judgment. When a task is underspecified, which is basically every real task, does the model ask the right question, make a reasonable assumption, or confidently go in the wrong direction? That's very hard to put into a number, but users feel it immediately.

The third is the distribution of failures rather than the average. Two models at 85% can fail on very different 15%. If one fails gracefully and the other fails in ways that are surprising or hard to detect, that matters a lot in practice.

So my honest view is that as models get stronger, evaluation becomes one of the most important research problems. In a sense, whoever defines the right next set of tasks, the ones that reflect real utility, is shaping where the whole field goes. The scores look similar right now partly because we're still measuring the last era's problems.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation needs better tasks that reflect real utility, but it does not identify specifying the desired model behavior as the harder issue when scores are similar.

r002.rationale: It notes that underspecified tasks call for judgment and that models can fail differently, but does not state that poorly defined desired behavior leads to differences evaluators did not anticipate.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that benchmark scores were never the thing we actually cared about. They were a proxy, and a proxy only works while the models are far enough apart that the proxy still separates them. Once everyone is at 90-something percent on the same handful of evals, the signal collapses, and you're left looking at the thing the benchmark was standing in for all along.

So what is that thing? For me it's how a model behaves when it has to act over time, not just answer once. A benchmark is a single-shot question with a known answer. Real usage is a long interaction with a user or an environment, where the model makes a decision, sees what happens, and makes another one. That's where the differences show up. One model recovers gracefully when a tool call fails, another one just keeps repeating the same thing. One model knows when it doesn't know and asks, another one confidently makes something up. None of that is captured by a static score, but it's exactly what determines whether you'd actually trust the model to do a task for you.

The second thing is that the evals we use are mostly things we already know how to grade. That's a selection effect. If there's a clean answer key, then by definition the task is one where humans already have the ground truth, and models converge on it. The interesting gaps between models are in the tasks where the answer isn't clean. Research, writing, engineering judgment, deciding what to do at all. Those are hard to evaluate, so they're underrepresented, so the scores look similar even when the models feel very different to use.

And honestly, "feel different to use" is not an unscientific statement. When people say a model has better taste, or is more reliable, or is more pleasant to work with over a long session, they're reporting a real measurement, it's just one we haven't figured out how to compress into a number yet. I think the next phase of evaluation is less about new question sets and more about building environments, letting models operate in them for a long time, and measuring outcomes at the end. That's much more expensive, but it's the only way the differences become visible again.

So my short answer: when scores converge, stop looking at scores. Look at trajectories, look at what happens on the hundredth step instead of the first, and look at the tasks nobody has written a grader for yet. That's where the models are still very different.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark scores are proxies and points to long interactions and hard-to-grade tasks, but it does not identify specifying what one wants the model to do as the harder issue.

r002.rationale: The response says differences show up on tasks that are hard to evaluate or lack graders, but it does not state that poorly defined desired behavior leads to differences the evaluator had not anticipated.

astra-6.text:
I think similar evaluation scores don’t necessarily mean the models have similar capabilities. A score compresses a lot of different behaviors into one number. Two models can get the same number of questions right while succeeding on quite different questions, or making very different kinds of mistakes.

And when you actually use them, other differences become visible. Does the model understand what you want when the instruction is ambiguous? Can it keep making progress on a task that takes many steps? If it makes a mistake, can it recognize that and recover? Those things aren’t necessarily captured by a benchmark where you give a question and grade the final answer.

So I would look at the models in the context of a particular task or system. For a coding assistant, for example, producing a good function is one thing; finding the relevant code, making a change, running tests, and responding to failures is another. Models with similar scores might behave quite differently across that process.

The evaluation scores are still useful. But as they get closer, we need more specific evaluations—and more experience using the models—to understand where the differences actually matter.

r001.rationale: It discusses ambiguous instructions and task-specific evaluation, but does not identify specifying what one wants the model to do as the harder issue.

r002.rationale: It notes that models differ in behaviors not captured by benchmarks, but does not state that poorly defined desired behavior leads to unanticipated differences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to ask is: similar on which evaluations? A benchmark measures a particular slice of capability. Once models get close on that slice, the score becomes less useful for understanding their differences. That doesn’t necessarily mean the models themselves have become equally capable.

For example, two models might both solve a programming problem, but one needs a very precise prompt, while the other can work through an ambiguous request, use tools, and recover when something goes wrong. If the evaluation only checks the final answer, those differences can be hard to see. But when you actually use them, they matter a lot.

So I would look at the kinds of tasks you can successfully delegate to each model, and how much supervision they require. Can it finish something that takes several steps? Can it recognize that its approach isn’t working? Does it ask for clarification at the right moment? There are also practical differences like latency and cost.

When scores become similar, we need to make the evaluation more representative of the work we actually want models to do. The important question becomes: under what conditions can I trust this model to complete a task?

r001.rationale: The response says to ask which evaluations matter and to make evaluations representative of intended work, but it does not identify specifying what one wants a model to do as the harder issue when scores are similar.

r002.rationale: The response notes that evaluations can miss differences between models, but it does not state that poorly defined desired behavior causes differences the evaluator did not anticipate.
